findings.title: Missing NULLing of conn_to_host.encalloc leads to double free on connection reuse
findings.message: In reuse_conn(), when an existing connection is reused, the `host` and `conn_to_host` struct hostname fields are moved (shallow-copied) from `old_conn` to `conn`. For `host`, both `rawalloc` and `encalloc` are correctly zeroed out on the source (`old_conn->host.rawalloc = NULL; old_conn->host.encalloc = NULL;`) after the copy, preventing the pointers from being freed twice. However, for `conn_to_host` only `rawalloc` is zeroed (`old_conn->conn_to_host.rawalloc = NULL;`) while `encalloc` is left untouched. Since `conn->conn_to_host = old_conn->conn_to_host;` is a shallow struct copy, both `conn->conn_to_host.encalloc` and `old_conn->conn_to_host.encalloc` now point at the same heap allocation. When `old_conn` is subsequently torn down (via conn_free(), which calls Curl_free_idnconverted_hostname() and frees `encalloc`), and later `conn->conn_to_host` is freed/reset (also via Curl_free_idnconverted_hostname(), e.g. on the next reuse or connection close), the same `encalloc` buffer is freed a second time, resulting in a double free / use-after-free that can be leveraged for memory corruption.
findings.suggestion: After copying old_conn->conn_to_host into conn->conn_to_host, fully clear the source struct (both rawalloc and encalloc, or the whole struct) so the moved-from connection no longer holds a live pointer to the transferred allocation. Best practice, as later adopted upstream, is to factor this move into a helper function that frees the destination's existing allocations, copies the struct, and then memsets the source struct to zero (or NULLs every pointer member) to fully sever ownership.

ground_truth.root_cause: Manual, ad-hoc 'move' semantics implemented by copying a struct and then individually NULLing out its pointer fields on the source is error-prone and was not applied consistently to all pointer members (`encalloc` was missed for `conn_to_host` while it was handled for `host`), leaving a dangling shared pointer between two structures.
